#151076. Industry News: A First Drive With the Fiat Topolino in Fresh York City

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1831 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: A First Drive With the Fiat Topolino in Fresh York City

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1831 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Fiat Topolino isn't exactly built for New York City.
  • It has a max speed of 25 miles per hour, a 46-mile range, and no airbags.
  • “It's a little bit of an experiment,” says Andrew Waterhouse, head of brand at Fiat USA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Fiat Topolino isn't exactly built for New York City. Fiat has been selling this tiny electric vehicle in Europe for three years, but it's now arriving in the US for $14,985 as a street-legal micromobility vehicle. Except it's more like a golf cart than a small EV.

It has a max speed of 25 miles per hour, a 46-mile range, and no airbags. Classified as a “Low Speed Vehicle (LSV),” it can only operate on roads with a posted speed limit of 35 mph or less. (You still need a driver's license, and the Topolino must be registered and have auto insurance.) It also doesn't have a traditional EV charging plug; instead, it uses a 10-foot AC plug that works in any wall outlet—which can be tough if you're in a Brooklyn apartment.

“It's a little bit of an experiment,” says Andrew Waterhouse, head of brand at Fiat USA. “This segment of micromobility—and that's really golf carts—based on the data we have, it's going to grow 28 percent in the next 5 years. People are driving golf carts not to play golf—they're driving them to go to the beach, to go to the clubhouse, to go get coffee, dinner, but they're all just generic. Topolino adds a little bit of that Italian flair and charm, and it's just so unique.”.

According to recent reports, that’s hard to refute. There's nothing like the Topolino on the market, EV or otherwise. Its adorable looks have drawn the attention of passersby, who've flicked me a thumbs up as I drove past, or pulled out their phones to sneak a quick pic. The Topolino (which is Italian for “little mouse,” and also what Italians call Mickey Mouse) comes with a lot of compromises, but I've had a blast piloting this thing around the city.

From my conversation with Waterhouse, it was clear that Fiat expects to sell more of these Topolino cars in places like suburban Florida. Gated communities, large residences with private land, homes by the beach—you get the idea. There are also hopes to turn the Topolino into a fleet vehicle for campuses and the like. But I wanted to see what it would be like in the bustling streets of New York City. After all, I already drive the Fiat 500 as my personal vehicle.

The Fiat Topolino, left, next to the already small Fiat 500, right.

The first thing that surprised me—other than the minuscule size, which you won't stop thinking about—is how plasticky the thing is. I leaned on it for a second and felt the plastic exterior sink in a little, which immediately made me realize the Topolino won't handle a crash very well; no crumple zones, no airbags—just seatbelts. So yes, don't take this thing on the highway.

Recent findings suggest that it's built for two people and not much else. The passenger can stow a suitcase in front of them, and there's a rack on the back of the car to store another. But besides mesh pouches in the door frames and an elongated glove compartment on top of the dashboard that runs the width of the car, that's about it for storage.

I should also mention the Topolino comes in a few variants: The standard model I tried has full doors and a fixed glass roof, but there's an Open Air model with a roll-back soft-top roof, and the Dolce Vita model has rope doors (aka no doors) and the soft-top roof. You can buy the car in mint, orange, or brownish-gray.

In a recent development, thankfully, despite my 6'4" frame, I fit quite comfortably in the Topolino. I do have to swing my leg under the steering wheel as I get in, and the seats are a little firm, but the inside feels quite roomy. Only the driver's seat can move forward or back—the passenger seat stays put, and you cannot adjust the steering wheel height.

The asymmetrical, reverse-hinged doors are very unique. The driver's side opens outward from the front, and the passenger door opens the opposite way. There's also a button on each side to open the door, and weirdly, to get out, you pull a fabric strap. Now, the driver-side strap is to the left of the steering wheel, which makes sense, but the passenger-side strap is in an awkward spot behind the seat, near the seatbelt strap. A few of my passengers found that annoying. Also annoying is that you need to use the key to unlock both doors individually—no auto-unlock button plus no key fob. (The car starts with a second key.).

Industry observers note that the horizontally split, manually hinged windows flip up, but on rougher roads, they tend to flip back down. You can adjust the small, circular side mirrors and the rear-view mirror, which also doubles as a backup camera display. I have found the backup camera mostly useless, especially at night, when it's just really hard to see what’s going on.

Good thing visibility in the Topolino is excellent, so it's really easy to swing your head around. Unsurprisingly, you can park this thing anywhere. I've parallel parked the Topolino in several tight spots that no other car can fit in, and the lack of parking sensors or the lackluster backup camera didn't bother me. In a city as crowded as Latest York, that's incredibly valuable.

You should know there's no air-conditioning or heating. There's a windshield fan to defog the windows, which, along with the single wiper and wiper fluid, was useful on cold, rainy days. But in the winter months, you'll have to bundle up, or in the summer, affix a battery-powered (or USB-C) fan to the dashboard. On the dash, you have a simple instrument cluster that shows speed and remaining range, and a built-in phone mount to the right.

You can store luggage on the rack—there's no trunk.

Turn the key to start the car, disengage the parking brake, and tap D or R to start driving. There's no power steering, so turning the wheel requires a little more force than you're used to, and the turn signals don't automatically disengage after you turn. Still, the car feels very responsive. The 8-horsepower electric motor feels fairly quick when you put the pedal to the metal, though you rapidly hit the Topolino’s top speed. Good thing the default speed limit in Fresh York City is 25 mph.

Sources indicate that but as you start driving, you'll experience arguably the worst thing about the Fiat Topolino: the sound. Because of federal regulations around electric LSVs, the Topolino has a pedestrian alert sound—the kind of angelic hum you might have heard when an electric car is reversing or rolling up to a stop sign. Except the sound is constant, and it gets louder the faster you go. I'm not sure why it's so loud in the car. It feels like it's alerting me more than pedestrians around me.

The sound only disappears if you go past 22 mph, which isn't often, since streets in most cities have a stop sign or traffic light after every block. The first time my wife and I rode in the car, we could barely hear each other talk over the hum. You get used to it over time, but it's very annoying. You can try playing music over it, but the car has no speaker system. Instead, Fiat sells a pair of Monster Bluetooth speakers that you can magnetically stick to the top frame of the car. That works OK, but I didn't like having to keep them charged, so when they died, I played music from my phone. It was sad.

You can fit the Topolino anywhere!

The ride is a little stiff. I drove over one of the worst roads in Brooklyn (Broadway), and you could feel every single bump. When I drove with my brother, they often just exclaimed “Jesus!” every few minutes. Cobblestone was equally pretty bad. But it's doable, and on well-maintained roads, the Topolino was a smooth ride.

Newly introduced Yorkers rejoice! You legally cannot drive this car into New Jersey. (As if you needed a reason.) All of the bridges and tunnels to the Garden State have speed limits higher than 35 mph. However, I could take the East River bridges to go from Brooklyn to Manhattan, and I did exactly that. Driving over the Manhattan Bridge was a little terrifying when I was holding up a few cars in my lane and everyone decided to race around me. But I got a few thumbs-ups along the way, which helped. Everyone finds this car cute, which goes a long way toward how people treat you on the road.

As for range, it's not great. I wish it were closer to 80 miles instead of 46 miles, especially at this price. It's perfect for quick hour-long round trips around the city; anything longer will give you range anxiety. That trip over the bridge? I went from Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, to Lower Manhattan and back (around 12 miles). The indicated remaining range went from 46 miles to 30 by the time I got home.

Recharging takes around five hours from zero to full, and the charging cord is built into the car near the passenger-side door. Annoyingly, the 10-foot cable isn't retractable, so you awkwardly have to stuff it back into the door frame when you're done. But the bigger issue is the length. And the standard AC plug. EV charging stations don't typically have AC outlets like the ones in your home. And 10 feet is far too short to reach any apartment or residence in New York City.

Charging the Fiat Topolino requires a standard wall outlet—and, in Brooklyn, probably a long extension cord.

It has been revealed that I bought a 50-foot extension cord and ran the cable from my outdoor parking spot to my backyard outlet. It worked perfectly well, but I'm also an outlier, with access to a parking spot and a backyard. Most people don't have those luxuries, so you'll need your own solution.

Recent findings suggest that initially, after my first ride with the Topolino, I was apprehensive. It felt like I was sitting in a plastic box on wheels, with a blaring sound that wouldn't stop, and every massive bump sending a shock into my body. After a week, I was driving the thing everywhere, hand dangling out the half-window, fist-bumping other drivers in bumper-to-bumper traffic, and parking in the tiniest available spots around Brooklyn. Now, a week without the little mouse, I miss it dearly.

In a recent development, it's far from the perfect city car. There are small things I would change to improve the overall rideability. And like the Fiat 500e, it's way too expensive. But as someone who likes their car to stand out, I find so much of what's available in the US market uninspiring. The Topolino breaks the mold. We need more small cars like it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The November full moon rose to put on a spectacular natural light show on Nov.
  • It has been revealed that each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names, often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising.
  • November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons, which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The November full moon rose to put on a spectacular natural light show on Nov. 24 and we've got the photos to prove it! Read on to see our favorite shots of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world.

It has been revealed that each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names, often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising. The November moon is often known as the Beaver Moon, a name associated with the time of year when beavers prepare for winter and when trappers historically set beaver traps before waterways froze.

November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons, which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.

That added proximity can make it appear noticeably brighter and larger than the smallest full moon of the year, setting the stage for an incredible photo shoot as the lunar disk climbed high into the autumn sky.

Our first shot of the moon was captured by photographer Pongmanat Tasiri as the moon rose over the roof of the Wat Phra That Doi Suthep Buddhist temple in Chiang Mai Province, Thailand, as a stunning array of craters and lunar seas scar the Beaver Moon's surface.

Meanwhile, Gary Hershorn snapped a gorgeous shot of the full yellow moon rising over the Chrysler Building in New York, with the Empire State Building and myriad other skyscrapers dominating the skyline.

Industry observers note that hershorn also managed to line up a colorful shot of the lunar disk glowing between the concrete canyon of Upcoming York's iconic 42nd Street just before moonset on the morning of Nov. 24, mere hours before the moon turned full.

NASA astronaut Anil Menon snapped a series of stunning photos from the International Space Station on Nov. 24, November full moon slipped out of view below Earth's horizon, while being gradually deformed by the warping effect of our planet's atmosphere. "Moonset today from space station - no edits to these photos from 400mm lens," Menon wrote in a post on X.

Heading back down to Earth Salih Zeki Fazlioglu took a colorful photo of the Beaver moon illuminating a thin veil of clouds above Istanbul, Turkiye, as reflected sunlight competed with the artificial glow of the city below for the viewer's attention.

This shot of the lunar disk looming over the Old Post Office Pavillion in Washington D.C. was captured by David Ake, with the pink sky complementing the orange and red leaves of autumn.

Recent findings suggest that our next photo was captured by Space.com's Skywatching Editor Daisy Dobrijevic using a Sony A7IV with a Tamron 50-400mm lens as the moon shone in the skies over the city of Nottingham in the U.K. on Nov. 23.

"Having seen the rather disappointing weather forecast for the night of the full moon, I decided to head out a day early and capture the almost-full Beaver Moon instead," explained Dobrijevic. "It hadn’t quite risen above the rooftops of the houses opposite me, so I took a peek down the alleyway and, sure enough, there it was, nestled between two houses, giving me just enough of a clear view to capture this close-up.".

This striking image of the full moon rising above the Toronto skyline was snapped by Mert Alper Dervis as a flock of birds skimmed through the foreground. The outline of the lunar disk appears subtly warped and squashed by atmospheric refraction, as its reflected light passes through pockets of air with differing densities and temperatures.

In a recent development, allen Berman sent in a breathtaking photo of the full moon hanging low over the Los Angeles skyline on the night of Nov. 24.

Sources indicate that "Finding the right spot for tonight’s full moon over downtown Los Angeles was a bit tricky," Berman told Space.com. "We wound up on a neighbor’s front lawn in the Baldwin Hills section of town. The owner was a bit surprised to see photographers there. But he was cool. The conditions were perfect with thin clouds over the distant mountains that made for a magical image.".

Moving from the modern to the old, photographer Robert Nemeti took a moody shot of the full Beaver Moon climbing skyward above the medieval Boldogkő Castle in Hungary at moonrise on Nov. 24. How many full moons must that old building have seen?

Wang Zhao snapped a very different view from Beijing, China, on that same night by using a powerful telephoto lens to capture a passenger jet as it streaked across the lunar disk, leaving dense contrails in its wake.

That Beaver Moon was captured shining between the minarets of the Imam Ali Shrine in the city of Najaf, Iraq, by Karar Essa. The 53-mile-wide (85-kilometer) Tycho Crater can be seen as a distinctive bright feature below the lunar equator, close to the dark expanse of Mare Nubium.

Aris Oikonomou snapped a striking photo of the Beaver Moon shining above the Parthenon in Athens, Greece, just as night began to set in over the Acropolis.

In a recent development, feeling inspired to capture your own supermoon photos? Then be sure to read our guide to photographing the moon and browse our picks of the best cameras and lenses for astrophotography because you don't have long to wait!

It has been revealed that the final supermoon of 2026 rises in just a few short weeks on Dec. 23 and it just so happens to be the closest full moon of the year, passing just 221,668 miles (356,740 kilometers) from Earth at the point of maximum illumination.

Republicans outspent Democrats for first time in over a decade in record 2026 midterm election political ad blitz

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (550 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence company AdImpact released Tuesday.
  • Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.
  • The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Political advertisers spent a record $12.06 billion during the 2025-26 elections, making it the first time a midterm cycle outspent a presidential cycle, according to a report from advertising intelligence company AdImpact released Tuesday.

Total spending exceeded AdImpact's June projection by more than $460 million.

The elections also marked the first time in over a decade that Republicans have outspent Democrats on advertisements, according to AdImpact.

Despite Republicans leading spending, John Link, senior vice president of data at AdImpact, said that "Dems still led or were generally even with overall airings and impressions.".

Recent findings suggest that the record spending extended across the board, with every type of race reaching a new high. Senate spending hit $3.39 billion, while spending on gubernatorial elections reached $2.61 billion, spending on races in the House of Representatives grew to $2.44 billion and state legislative races totaled $602 million, all records, according to AdImpact.

The 2026 midterm cycle was largely powered by megadonors, with SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk becoming the largest contributor by funneling more than $366 million into campaigns.

The biggest donors in this year's election disproportionately favored Republicans, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records. Fourteen out of the 20 largest donor groups supported GOP candidates, according to that analysis.

Republicans spent $5.51 billion on political advertisements, compared with $5.11 billion spent by Democrats, according to AdImpact.

While Republican spending increased by 27% from 2024, spending by Democrats fell by 4%.

Fundraisers told CNBC in interviews that Democratic donors' hesitancy largely stems from memories of Kamala Harris' defeat in 2024, unease about the rise of democratic socialism and distrust in party leadership.

Though they were outspent, Democrats made sweeping gains against Republicans in races nationwide, taking control of both the House and the Senate and flipping seats in some of the most competitive places, including Texas and Kansas.

According to recent reports, it is not the first time spending did not align with the winners. In 2024, President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Harris despite Democrats outspending Republicans.

While party majorities in Congress have switched hands, the most popular medium for political ads has not changed.

In a recent development, broadcast television represented the largest category for spending in this year's election, accounting for 49%, or $5.85 billion, of political ad spending, according to AdImpact. Broadcast's share of political ad dollars is up slightly from 48% in 2024.

Broadcast TV's strength comes despite facing pressure from falling viewership and increasing competition from streaming.

In a recent development, industry experts have told CNBC that political advertisers continue to spend on broadcast because it reaches local markets and active voting populations. The Associated Press also reported that airtime was so expensive during the midterm elections that some candidates, including Republican Ken Paxton in Texas, bought ads during national sporting events, figuring that reaching enough constituents through a national broadcast might actually be less expensive than buying across the state's local television markets.

Industry observers note that the fastest-growing categories in this year's cycle were connected TV, or internet-connected devices like Apple TV or Roku, with $2.66 billion, and digital, with $1.91 billion. Both mediums grew double digits from the 2024 presidential election. Spending on cable and radio declined 7% and 13%, respectively, from 2024.

Tech Report: 8 Best Keyboards (2026): My Honest Picks After Testing Dozens

📅 18 May 2019 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5667 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Regardless of how little you might think about yours, you probably use it every day.
  • Sources indicate that because we already have a separate guide focused on mechanical keyboards, this list instead places more focus on lower-profile keyboards and other non-mechanical options aimed at a more casual typist.
  • Be sure to check out our other peripheral guides for more, like the Best Mechanical Keyboards, Best Hall Effect Keyboards, Best Mouse, Best Ergonomic Mouse, and Best Computer Monitors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Keyboards are important. Regardless of how little you might think about yours, you probably use it every day. A keyboard that’s comfortable and easy to use is indispensable and helps you not only do good work—but enjoy doing it as well.

Sources indicate that because we already have a separate guide focused on mechanical keyboards, this list instead places more focus on lower-profile keyboards and other non-mechanical options aimed at a more casual typist. There’s a greater focus on typing comfort and efficiency, instead of typing feel, and less emphasis on customization options like hot-swap sockets or keycap accessibility.

Be sure to check out our other peripheral guides for more, like the Best Mechanical Keyboards, Best Hall Effect Keyboards, Best Mouse, Best Ergonomic Mouse, and Best Computer Monitors.

Industry observers note that updated Noember 2026: I've added the Wallhack K-001 and Keychron K2 HE Concrete Edition to my top recommendations, as well as the Keychron V6 Ultra 8K Hybrid to my honorable mentions. I've also included a couple of recent keyboards I've reviewed that I would suggest avoiding entirely.

One of the highlights of Keychron’s current lineup is its selection of mid-century-inspired keyboards with clean, simple designs and wood highlights. Instead of the standard gamer-y aesthetic, these keyboards offer a more refined style that looks at home on a professional’s desk. The K3 is the first low-profile keyboard in this series, offering a slimmer and more portable typing experience with the same fantastic design language. While this isn’t necessarily the best keyboard on this list by any one metric, I think it’s the most practical option for the largest number of people.

In a recent development, there are two versions of the K3: The typing-focused Ultra and the gaming-focused HE. The Ultra uses standard low-profile mechanical switches, with options for either linear Red switches, or tactile Brown or Banana switches. These switches can be swapped out without any soldering thanks to the hot-swap sockets on the PCB. The switches and stabilizers come lubed from the factory, resulting in typing that feels smooth and offers a consistent, rattle-free sound when typing.

Sources indicate that the HE offers only linear Hall effect switches, but these allow for more advanced software customization, such as adjustable actuation distances (how far you press the switch before it registers an input) and Rapid Trigger (which allows for more rapid keypresses by detecting the direction of the switch’s movement). While the enhanced customization of a Hall effect switch is great for gaming, the adjustability won’t be worth the added cost and loss of switch customization for the average user.

The only trade-off with this keyboard is that, compared to a full-size mechanical keyboard, it does lose some travel distance; a low-profile switch is 3.1 mm total, compared with a standard switch’s 4.0 mm. This can be preferable for consumers who prefer a snappier typing experience or who prioritize a compact form factor.

Both models share the same compact form factor, stylish design, and open-source QMK software for customization, along with the ability to use Keychron’s web-based Launcher for adjusting key mapping and RGB lighting colors.

It has been revealed that with Gateron-made KS-TR Hall effect switches and a design that looks straight out of a Dieter Rams–era Braun catalog, I absolutely love this keyboard. The typing experience is fantastic, and this keyboard has a presence on your desk that not many others can match. While the K-001 doesn’t feature a bouncy gasket-mount design, the “stack mount” system it uses (similar to the Wooting 60HE V2 listed below) creates a stiffer, consistent typing feel across the entire keyboard, which I prefer for regular typing.

It has been revealed that beyond that, the K-001 features specs that are competitive with quite a few high-end gaming offerings, with customizable settings for switch actuation distance, rapid trigger functionality, and extensive programmability. It even boasts an 8,000-Hz polling rate and 0.125-millisecond input latency, making it a fantastic choice for even the most competitive gaming. Really, the only thing missing is wireless connectivity, but that’s not a major issue for a gaming-focused keyboard with a hefty CNC aluminum shell.

Another small detail I love is the lighting on this keyboard. Each of the switches is designed to carefully guide the LED underneath to only shine behind the lettering, without any light bleeding between the keys. The LEDs themselves are a well-balanced, neutral white, as opposed to the multicolored RGB found in most keyboards (which often gain a very bluish tint when set to pure white). This all results in a much more minimal and tasteful LED setup compared to the ultra-bright, sometimes overwhelming offerings from other manufacturers.

While the price point is high, especially compared to offerings from more cost-conscious brands like Keychron, this keyboard really is a great object to hold and use, and one that has incredibly robust construction and great engineering underneath the hood.

According to recent reports, keychron’s B2 Pro is one of the best scissor-switch keyboards available, mainly because of the customization it allows. This keyboard uses Keychron’s Launcher, an in-browser software that provides extensive and intuitive customization options for its keyboards, with everything from remapping and macros to multiple function layers. For any type of productivity work, this level of customization can be a great way to optimize an already-good keyboard to one that's perfect for your regular tasks, whether that’s mapping multimedia controls to a function layer or having specific key combinations ready at a moment’s notice.

It has been revealed that this keyboard offers a good typing experience for the price, using low-profile scissor switches with a short and snappy key press without being particularly loud or disruptive. The case is made entirely of plastic, and the keycaps are subtly sculpted with a dish (similar to Logitech’s MX Keys line), which makes finding the center of a keycap easier when touch-typing. Because of the low-profile scissor switches, the B2 Pro still feels like a laptop keyboard at the end of the day, which can seem lacking if you’re coming from something with a more robust design.

Recent findings suggest that slim, durable, and highly customizable, Razer’s Joro is pretty much the most compact gaming keyboard you can find today. It’s thinner than a laptop and just barely thicker than an iPhone, and has the same footprint as a standard 60 percent keyboard, meaning it can slip easily into a backpack, tote bag, or even a large purse. If you were really dedicated, I’m sure it could even fit in the pocket of some cargo pants. The Joro uses Razer’s Synapse software, an incredibly powerful and intuitive customization app that lets you control the keyboard’s RGB lighting, remap any of its keys, and program macros with ease.

It has been revealed that the only significant downside of this keyboard is the lack of a 2.4-GHz dongle. This means the keyboard can connect only to devices via Bluetooth or a wired connection. While this isn’t a deal-breaker for me, since the device still has multi-device Bluetooth connectivity, it does slightly hinder the keyboard’s functionality.

In many ways, the Mchose GX87 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is a “mini” version of the WobKey Crush 80. It has the same layout with similar design choices, and it uses comparable switches and an identical gasket-mount system. However, the GX87 misses out on some of the fancier features of the Crush 80. The colors are e-coated instead of anodized on most models (which creates a less smooth texture), the case is lighter and simpler, and disassembly is generally more complicated.

Sources indicate that however, this keyboard still feels great to type on, especially at its budget-minded starting price. If you’re less concerned about some of the style or convenience aspects of a keyboard but still want something that feels great while you're typing, the GX87 is one of the best options available from a per-dollar standpoint. (There are three variants: Lite, Max, and Ultra. Aside from how the colors are coated, the Ultra uses a different switch and has a quick-disassemble design.).

According to recent reports, contrary to what you’d expect from the conceptual absurdity of a concrete keyboard, the Keychron K2 HE (8/10, WIRED Recommends) is genuinely delightful. The design is a bit silly, but that doesn’t get in the way of the performance or the usability of this keyboard. And more importantly, underneath the concrete housing and color-matched keycaps, the internals of this keyboard both feel fantastic to type on (smooth, buttery switches and a solid mounting system make it rigid without feeling harsh) and put down some great specs (2.4-GHz wireless with 8,000-Hz polling and fully customizable Hall effect switches).

Sources indicate that but really, what I like best is the material. Using concrete for a keyboard is a bit tongue-in-cheek, and incredibly reminiscent of Soviet-era brutalist architecture—and it won me over. The K2 HE ends up becoming as much of a “Hey, check this out” conversation piece as it is an actual keyboard, and during testing, it put a smile on my face every time I went to use it. That has to count for something doesn't it?

I really don’t understand how Keychron can make a keyboard that has mechanical switches, high-quality keycaps, RGB lighting, and an 8,000-Hz polling rate for under $60. It just doesn’t add up to me. But the manufacturer did it, and the resulting keyboard is really fantastic. If you want something with retro styling, comfortable keycaps, and a satisfying typing sound, you really can’t get a better per-dollar value proposition than the C1 Pro. Keychron’s tactile Super Banana switches are poppy and responsive, and the tray-mount case feels sturdy when typing. The only caveat, and this is hardly an glitch for most consumers, is that this keyboard doesn’t have wireless connectivity.

Industry observers note that compared with quite a few other budget-minded keyboards, Keychron’s software is entirely usable and regularly updated. I’ve used quite a few sub-$100 mechanical keyboards with subpar software, with challenges ranging from a lack of customization and poor translation to a complete inability to run without hours of troubleshooting. Meanwhile, Keychon Launcher works in-browser, boots up perfectly, allows for extensive customizations, and connects in seconds every time.

It has been revealed that the Wooting 60HE is a fantastic keyboard, and the v2 manages to improve on it in almost every way. The polling rate is upped to 8,000 Hz, the switches are updated, and the mounting method has been significantly modernized from the previous tray-mounted design, instead using an isolation mount that both feels better and has a softer typing sound. Plus, the 60HE v2 is one of the few Hall effect keyboards available with a split spacebar, which can be great for both gaming and productivity once you’ve adapted to it.

Sources indicate that while it lacks wireless connectivity, basically every other aspect of this keyboard is as good as it gets: The 60 percent layout uses standard designs that are common in the aftermarket, allowing for easy upgrades to the case, and the v2 is one of the few mainstream Hall effect keyboards to use a standardized type of switch, meaning it can be easily swapped out with countless aftermarket options. In-software customization of actuation distance, multi-input, and quite a few other cutting-edge settings means you won’t be wanting for gaming performance, either. The only thing to watch out for is the compact 60 percent layout, which saves a lot of space but won’t be for everyone.

Sources indicate that keychron V6 Ultra 8K Hybrid for $164: By introducing a true “hybrid” keyboard, Keychron has resolved its largest matter with Hall effect keyboards: lack of customization. Along with being compatible with standard MX-style mechanical switches, Keychron also claims the V6 is compatible with “95 percent of mechanical switches on the market.” Although it’s hard to prove that number exactly, this opens up a vast world of customization possibilities, along with providing significantly more options for repairs in the event of a switch failing. Beyond this, it also means you can have access to both mechanical switches with a tactile bump and highly customizable Hall-effect switches without needing two keyboards.

In a recent development, happy Hacking Keyboard Classic Type-S for $222: The Happy Hacking Keyboard lineup has never been known for cost-effectiveness. This is shown especially with the Pro Classic Type-S, a nearly-$300 keyboard with wired-only connectivity and a distinct lack of bells and whistles. However, the unique layout and Topre switches can pretty much only be found here, and make for a unique tactile typing experience that can’t be matched by many other keyboards. Plus, the massive aftermarket community for Topre keyboards means both repair and customization are incredibly easy and well-documented. They’re a bit pricey, but one of these keyboards could last the rest of your life with a bit of care.

Wooting 80HE for $200: While the technology falls a bit behind the 60HE V2, the 80HE’s larger layout still makes it a fantastic option for anyone who isn’t quite ready to get rid of their F-row and arrow keys. The switches feel great, the magnesium case is incredibly robust, and the Wootility customization interface is both straightforward and incredibly powerful.

Sources indicate that logitech Pro X TKL for $140: Logitech makes great keyboards, and the G Pro X TKL is among the best gaming keyboards. It has vibrant RGB LED-backlit keys, a choice of clicky, tactile, or linear switches, and it uses Logitech’s Lightspeed wireless adapter for competitive gaming-level response time. The build quality of this keyboard is slick and stylish. It’s minimal and doesn't take up much space on your desk, and it has a subtle metallic rim around the edge that gives it a little flair that most plain keyboards lack. The volume wheel in the upper right is smooth and easy to reach, and along the top are handy media controls so you can pause your music when you finally get into a game after a long queue. For my tastes, the more clicky-clacky a keyboard, the better, and the Black Clicky switches have served me well. Each keypress feels like I'm sending tiny thunder down to my game. However, if you prefer something softer, you can choose another switch type. The only thing I dislike is the lack of a numpad—yes, I’m one of those weirdos who prefer having a numpad.

Logitech Pro X 60 for $130: The Pro X 60 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) has virtually all the benefits of the Pro X TKL in a smaller, more compact package. It keeps the volume wheel, Game mode switch, and Bluetooth/Lightspeed buttons by moving them to the edges of the keyboard, while slimming the whole thing down to a 60 percent layout.

Sources indicate that logitech Pop Keys for $67: The Pop Keys (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is a vibrant line of wireless keyboards that come in a wide variety of color palettes that are delightful. It also uses Logitech's system for pairing with up to three devices, making it simple to take it between your PC and laptop, or from home to work and back.

Sources indicate that logitech MX Keys S for $110: The MX Keys S can pair with three devices, making it easy to swap between computers. Its low-profile chiclet-style keys are comfortable, and it uses proximity sensors to activate the key backlight when your hands get near, so it's easier to see in the dark without wasting battery when you’re not using it. It supports both Mac and Windows layouts, and the keys are tastefully labeled in a way that it’s clear no matter which one you’re using at the time. Battery life is also fantastic, lasting well over a week with normal use, though it gets quite a bit longer life if you disable the backlight.

Sources indicate that logitech MX Mechanical for $142: With an understated, low-profile design, you can pair the MX Mechanical with up to three devices at once and swap with the push of a button. There are even a few convenient extra buttons just above the numpad to launch a calculator or lock your desktop.

It has been revealed that turtle Beach Vulcan II TKL Pro for $150: The Vulcan II TKL Pro has two LEDs per key, giving it a better resolution for lighting effects. It features Hall effect switches, which should cut down on wear and tear. They’re still satisfyingly clicky, and the volume knob has a comfortably grippy texture. I prefer any keyboard with a volume wheel to one without.

It has been revealed that corsair K65 Plus for $100: This 75 percent keyboard has some of the softest, most comfortable keys of any board I’ve tested. It’s lightweight enough to toss in a bag but sturdy enough to be your desktop keyboard. It can connect via USB-C, Bluetooth, or a wireless dongle that can be stored in a slot on the rear. A stylish metal volume knob adorns the top-right corner, and every keycap and switch can be swapped out using the included removal tool.

Razer Huntsman Mini for $65: A 60 percent keyboard has 60 percent of the keys normally found on a regular-size keyboard. The numpad and arrow keys are chopped off, and you’re left with the essentials. The Razer Huntsman Mini is one of my favorites of this size for gaming. It feels every bit as responsive and quick as a full-size keyboard, but it takes up a lot less desk space. There’s just something neat and orderly about it. Plus, like the larger Huntsman Elite, the Mini is compatible with Razer’s keycap kits, so you can customize your color scheme.

Sources indicate that keychron Q1 HE for $212: The Keychron Q1 HE (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is one of the best boards we’ve tested that uses Hall effect switches. You can customize the actuation point to either make keys more sensitive—so you don’t have to press them all the way down for keystrokes to register—or less sensitive, to avoid those fat-finger moments that can ruin competitive games. Keychron even has rapid-trigger settings that allow you to press a key multiple times without the key having to return fully to its resting position. Even outside the benefits of the Hall effect switches, this is another great keyboard in line with the kind that Keychron is known for, so it’s worth a look even if you don’t want to pay that much attention to every aspect of your keys.

According to recent reports, NZXT Function 2 for $50: The original NZXT Function was a great way for anyone interested in mechanical keyboards to jump in without getting overwhelmed. The follow-up Function 2 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) improves on it in almost every way. It upgrades the keys to optical switches and comes with a spare set of switches that have a little more (or a little less) resistance, so you can customize specific keys based on your needs. I found this particularly useful for games like Overwatch 2, where I’d like to cut down on those fat-finger ultimates that are so embarrassing. The Function 2 retains many of my favorite features from the first model. It has the same left-side volume roller, super-soft keycaps, and convenient buttons along the side of the keyboard. If you’re interested in mechanical keyboards but are intimidated by phrases like “actuation force,” this is a great board to get started with.

Razer Huntsman V3 Pro TKL for $132: The Huntsman V3 Pro TKL is a robust keyboard for those who like to tweak their gaming setup. It uses Razer’s analog optical switches, which are satisfyingly clicky. On the top right, there’s a media knob that controls the volume, which you can also click to mute. However, it’s the buttons around it that are most interesting. To the left, there are two programmable macro keys you can use to customize different commands for your games (or your work). Below, on the navigation keys, are six profile shortcuts. Hold Fn and press one of them, and you can swap between several preset profiles, tailored to specific gaming needs like FPS mode, Racing mode, or High-Sensitivity mode when you need to pull off that hair trigger. All of this can be customized in the Razer Synapse app. We’ve tested a lot of keyboards with different customization options, but this one is particularly good for gamers who swap profiles a lot. The keyboard connects using a USB-C cable, included with the device, and it also comes with a magnetic wrist rest.

Razer BlackWidow V4 75% for $126: The Razer BlackWidow V4 (8/10, WIRED Recommends) has a sturdy metal casing, hot-swappable switches, and Razer’s robust Synapse software for customizing your keyboard. It’s also earned our top marks if you’re looking for a mechanical keyboard specifically for gaming. The 75 percent layout is small enough that you can leave plenty of room for your mouse, making those flicks to land a headshot that much easier in competitive games. The 8,000-Hz polling rate also helps cut down on the times that you miss activating an ability by that almost imperceptible fraction of a second.

Industry observers note that steelSeries Apex Pro for $150: Rather than choose one switch for the Apex Pro keyboard, SteelSeries decided to allow them all. Not only is it a colorful gaming keyboard with lots of bells and whistles, but it also features mechanical switches that can be customized per key to give you a typing experience unique to you. Plus, it has a little LED display for system alerts, volume, and other fun stuff you can toy with using SteelSeries’ included software.

Logitech G512 X 98: While a hybrid mechanical/Hall effect keyboard may sound like a great all-around solution, it really only works as a regular keyboard when the feeling between the switches stays consistent. That’s exactly where this keyboard falls short: The “tactile” model I tested only had mechanical switches with a tactile bump, while the Hall effect switches were linear. When trying to type or do other productivity work, the two ended up constantly clashing. This means you either have to put up with an unpleasant typing experience or you’ll always have to swap out switches and recalibrate when moving between work and play.

Recent findings suggest that razer Pro Type Ergo: While this keyboard is solid and feels good to type on, the $200 price point seems far too high for what it is. Having a plastic case and laptop-like chiclet-style 66 keys, it won’t blow your socks off. Unless you desperately need Chroma RGB lighting, or have some other reason to stay within the Razer ecosystem, there are much more affordable options that offer nearly identical usability.

What Kinds of Keyboards Are There?

It has been revealed that generally, keyboards are defined by two specific design choices: the layout and the type of switches they use. A switch is the mechanism underneath a key that controls how the switch is pressed down. The layout can easily be seen by looking at a keyboard, but the switches can be a bit more difficult to guess from general observation. Here are the most common you’ll see:.

In a recent development, scissor switches are among the most widespread types of keyboard switches available today, found in nearly every consumer laptop and countless slim keyboards, including the Apple Magic Keyboard. These switches are incredibly compact and have a short travel distance, which makes them ideal for anything portable. Their low profile, flat shape, and short travel distance means they can be quick to type on, but they often lack the enjoyable tactile experience of a thicker keyboard. These switches are often also referred to as chiclet switches, a not-quite-accurate name that comes from the small amount of space between each key.

Recent findings suggest that membrane switches are one of the least expensive switches to manufacture, and are widespread even today in schools and offices. They typically consist of a sheet of rubber domes with electrical contacts inside of them, which then have keycaps put on top. When one of these keys is pressed down, it compresses the rubber dome and registers a key press. These keyboards are waterproof and reliable, but they have a key press that is typically described as mushy and unpleasant.

Industry observers note that mechanical switches are fairly widespread in enthusiast circles, but the actual definition of a “mechanical” switch is debatable. However, for this guide’s purpose, a “mechanical switch” will typically refer to a switch that uses the same design as a Cherry MX switch and has a metal “leaf” on the inside, which is two pieces of metal that are pressed together to register an input. ThereminGoat has a great in-depth guide on how a mechanical switch works and what all the components do. There are three main types of MX-style mechanical switches, tactile, linear, and clicky, that we discuss in-depth in our mechanical keyboard buying guide.

Low-profile mechanical switches rely on principles similar to a standard mechanical switch, but they compress the movement into a much shorter switch. They typically have a shorter key press, use unique keycaps, and are less standardized than full-size mechanical switches. Because they’re shorter, they are typically used for either low-profile keyboards or uniquely shaped keys on a standard keyboard (like the mouse buttons on the HHKB Studio).

It has been revealed that hall effect switches are typically similar to mechanical switches in shape, and will feel comparable to type on, but the key difference is how they register an input. A mechanical switch requires physical contact between two components, while a Hall effect switch uses magnets and sensors to determine whether a key has been pressed down. With most Hall effect keyboards, the sensor can detect how far the key has been pressed, and you can actually program the keys to only register an input at a certain distance, or even to register multiple inputs at different distances. By comparison, a standard mechanical switch will only register an input at a predetermined distance. While a Hall effect switch may seem like an all-around upgrade compared to a mechanical switch, there is still a trade-off: Nearly every Hall effect switch available is linear, which means there is no bump or click when the keyboard registers an input. Beyond that, because of small differences in their internal designs, many enthusiasts prefer the typing feel of a mechanical switch.

There are so many factors to consider when picking the right keyboard for your needs that it can get overwhelming. Not everyone has the same needs, and many aspects of a keyboard can seem universally desirable to some while being utterly polarizing to others. Here are a few things to keep in mind:.

According to recent reports, mechanical, or no? If you like significant, clicky keyboards with raised keys that make a statement, mechanical keyboards might be for you. This is also a rabbit hole that many nerds have lost themselves in, so it can be overwhelming to dive into the nuance of all the different styles in this subgroup. If you’re more a fan of the flat, chiclet-style keyboards found on low-profile keyboards (and laptops), you can save yourself a lot of time by skipping the mechanical keyboard rush. On the other hand, if you do want mechanical, we have a few in this guide you can check out, but we also have a dedicated Best Mechanical Keyboard guide you should peruse.

Wireless or wired? Wired keyboards have the advantage of never dying and never needing to be charged up. The disadvantages are, well, obvious. If you need a wireless keyboard to take with you to the office and back home, or just want more flexibility on your desk, then make sure to check a keyboard's battery life, what kind of batteries it uses (rechargeable is usually better), and what kind of system it uses for recharging.

Wireless connectivity options. Some wireless keyboards use a 2.4-GHz USB dongle to connect to your PC or laptop, which often means more reliable signal strength, while others use Bluetooth to connect to a wider range of devices. Bluetooth keyboards in general are pretty great these days, so it’s not a huge sacrifice, but pay attention to how you need to connect the keyboard to your devices when making a purchase.

Industry observers note that number of device connections. Similarly, some wireless keyboards can remember multiple devices they connect to and swap between them with the press of a button. If you have a desktop, a laptop, and a work computer you want to use one keyboard with, it’s a good idea to check how many devices your keyboard can remember when making your choice.

It has been revealed that polling rate. As mentioned, this refers to how often per second your computer receives a signal from your keyboard. Modern keyboards already approach 1,000 Hz (or once every millisecond), which is faster than what most people ever need. However, if you play a lot of fast-paced competitive games online, having a higher polling rate (commonly approaching 8,000 Hz, or eight checks every millisecond) can reduce the time between when you press a key and when the game registers it. Which, when you're dodging headshots, can mean the difference between life and virtual death.

In a recent development, software. With most keyboards today advertising extensive customization options, it’s crucial to be sure these adjustments can be done easily and quickly. Some keyboards have great customization software with explanations, tool tips, and intuitive systems to make adjustments, and some don’t. Software like Razer Synapse, Keychron’s Launcher, and Wooting’s Wootility are some of my favorites, and I’d definitely recommend doing some research on your keyboard’s software before locking in your choice.

The Keyboard Terms You Should Know.

It has been revealed that hz, or hertz, refers to the polling rate of a keyboard. In essence, this number is how many times the keyboard communicates with your computer in one second. Your average computer peripheral operates at 125 Hz, while higher-end equipment with a focus on speed can operate upwards of 1,000 Hz. Realistically, for everyday use, 125 Hz is perfectly serviceable. Having something higher can be beneficial for gaming, and can potentially feel smoother, but the difference is not as important as you would think.

Industry observers note that 2.4 GHz, short for 2.4 gigahertz, is a radio frequency that computer peripherals use to communicate wirelessly with a USB dongle. Most keyboards with 2.4-GHz connectivity will also have Bluetooth connectivity, but there are many keyboards that have Bluetooth without 2.4 GHz. There are many differences between how the two operate and how they perform, but the main ones are connection quality and convenience. A Bluetooth connection will often operate at a lower polling rate, such as 125 Hz or 250 Hz, but can connect directly to a Bluetooth-enabled device without a dongle. A 2.4-GHz connection, on the other hand, can operate at much higher polling rates (some devices exceed 1,000 Hz) but will require a USB port to plug a dongle into. For either connection method, the wireless range is dependent on the individual device.

According to recent reports, gasket mounting is a method of keyboard construction that has become popular in recent years. In a gasket-mounted keyboard, the internal assembly of the keyboard is not directly screwed into the case. Instead, rubber gaskets are placed along the edges of the top and bottom halves of the case. These press together around the internal assembly and hold it in place once the two halves have been screwed together. This allows the internal assembly to move up and down slightly when typing, along with absorbing the vibrations of typing. This kind of assembly typically results in a softer and more satisfying typing experience, while also improving the sound of the keyboard by removing any extra noises.

In a recent development, function layers are secondary layouts on a keyboard that allow for inputs that don’t have dedicated keys on the keyboard. These are often accessed by holding down a key labeled “Fn” or “Function,” then pressing another key. Function layers allow for multimedia controls, setting adjustments, or access to keys like F1 through F12, or arrow keys, if they were removed from the keyboard to save space.

I test each keyboard on this list for an extended period of time: at least a week, and often longer. I test each under a diverse set of conditions including gaming, writing, internet browsing, video and photo editing, and even some programming. During this, I take extensive notes on how a keyboard behaves, what works, and where I run into trouble. Once I’ve finished testing a keyboard in real-life situations, I compare it to other keyboards to see how it stacks up, and I typically try to disassemble each keyboard and critique its internal assembly.

In a recent development, when determining what goes in this guide, I take multiple different aspects into account. The largest priorities to me are build quality, typing experience, and ease-of-use: A solid keyboard that feels good to type on will typically score better than a flimsy and boring keyboard, even if the flimsy keyboard has fantastic software, style, or typing sound. However, all of these metrics come into consideration, and if a keyboard totally fails in a certain category, that can still take it out of the running.

Keyboards are subjective, so I try to approach each review with an open mind. Even if I don’t like typing on a keyboard, I always try to imagine a user who might like it, and I evaluate its design choices from that perspective along with my own. Ultimately, you will know better than anyone else whether a keyboard is a good fit for you.

Latest Update: Astronomers discover the most distant and ancient supermassive black hole-powered quasar in the universe

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Euclid space telescope has spotted the most distant and ancient quasar ever seen, a bright cosmic event powered by a supermassive black hole with 360 million times the mass of the sun.
  • The supermassive black hole is seen as it was just 630 million years after the Major Bang.
  • The discovery further deepens the mystery of how supermassive black holes grew so massive so soon into the history of the universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Euclid space telescope has spotted the most distant and ancient quasar ever seen, a bright cosmic event powered by a supermassive black hole with 360 million times the mass of the sun.

The supermassive black hole is seen as it was just 630 million years after the Major Bang. 40 million years further back in time than the previous record holder for the most ancient quasar.

The discovery further deepens the mystery of how supermassive black holes grew so massive so soon into the history of the universe. That's because previously, scientists had theorized it should take 1 billion years of feeding and merging for black holes to reach supermassive status of millions or billions of times as massive as the sun.

Industry observers note that quasars occur when supermassive black holes are surrounded by vast amounts of gas and dust on which they feed. The immense gravitational influence of the black hole causes this material, in the form of an accretion disk, to glow brightly and to blast out bright jets of plasma. That means quasars at the heart of galaxies in regions called active galactic nuclei (AGNs) like this one can often be brighter than the combined light of every star in the entire surrounding galaxy, but only briefly.

The newly discovered quasar, designated J1504+6252 and nicknamed Dún Aonghasa, is in this brief phase of its existence. It was discovered among millions of objects in 18 months of data from Euclid.

Sources indicate that euclid's initial observation of Dún Aonghasa was followed up by an array of ground-based and space-based telescopes, including the W.M. Keck Observatory, the Large Binocular Telescope Observatory, the Hubble Space Telescope, and ultimately the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). It was the JWST that determined the mass of this supermassive black hole.

In a recent development, what is interesting about Dún Aonghasa is that it is unlike other supermassive black holes seen at a similar period of the early universe. That's because this black hole is feeding relatively slowly. That means if it engaged in rapid feeding to reach its massive size, that period of gorging on gas and dust has either ended or it has paused.

That is something that further complicates our picture of supermassive black hole growth.

By staring back 13.1 billion years in time to see Dún Aonghasa, Euclid is also observing a crucial time in cosmic history when the first stars and galaxies were taking shape, and the clearing of cosmic gas was ending the dark ages of our universe by allowing light to travel freely.

According to recent reports, euclid's primary mission is improving our understanding of dark energy, the mysterious force accelerating the expansion of the universe, and dark matter, the most mysterious "stuff" in the cosmos. Collectively, these aspects of the universe account for around 95% of its matter-energy budget and have come to be collectively referred to as the dark universe. Hence Euclid's nickname as the "dark universe detective.".

This research, along with Euclid's discovery of at least 12 that date back around 13 billion years, shows that this pioneering space telescope launched in 2023 could also make a major contribution to our understanding of black holes and their growth.

Recent findings suggest that the team's research was published on Tuesday (Nov. 24) in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

Hanna Hattab has refereed in a number of competitions run by the Asian Football Confederation.

Claims that a referee was drunk during an Asian Football Confederation (AFC) Champions League Two match are "entirely unfounded", officials say.

Syrian referee Hanna Hattab was replaced at half-time of the match between Iran's Gol Gohar and Al Jazira of the United Arab Emirates.

Reports claimed Gol Gohar staff accused the referee of being drunk following what has been described as some erratic decision-making in the first half.

Iranian news agency ISNA quoted one club official as saying: "The referee was not in a normal state," and suggesting they would not have played on had the referee not been removed.

Accusations of drunkenness were also widely shared on social media.

But Hattab, who is part of the AFC's elite refereeing group, has released a statement denying the allegation, saying he has been defamed and threatening legal action.

The fourth official took over for the second half, with Al Jazira winning the match.

Hattab said he will be "issuing an official statement that clarifies all the details and facts related to what happened".

Omani sports journalist Issa Stated, who covers Asian competitions, claimed on social media that what happened to Hattab was "due to a drop in his blood sugar, which caused him to lose concentration and focus".

"He underwent a medical examination after the match and was not intoxicated, contrary to what has been circulating.".

In their statement on the match, which was played in Asia's second tier continental competition, the Syrian Football Association backed Hattab.

"Following an assessment of his health, it has been confirmed - contrary to various claims circulating on social media - that the reports regarding his situation are entirely unfounded," they wrote.

"The Committee reiterates its unwavering support for him and is committed to thoroughly investigating all details and circumstances surrounding the incident.".

A new book charts the complicated relationship between the two legends, starting on a sunny afternoon in Rio in 1979.

Sources indicate that pelé and Diego Maradona first met in April 1979, four months before the Argentinian led his country’s under-20 side to victory at the World Youth Cup. Maradona told a journalist friend that his dream was to meet the Brazilian, and after a few weeks of aborted attempts to bring them together – mostly because Diego did not want to travel on a Monday, the one day he had free for his girlfriend Claudia – the meeting finally took place in Rio.

Industry News: Here’s Everything You Can Do With With the New Gemini AI on Android Auto

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that google Assistant is being replaced by Google’s more advanced Gemini AI across all platforms, and that includes Android Auto.
  • You’ll see a message onscreen announcing the arrival of Gemini, with the latest “spark” icon (a small star by a sound-wave-like icon), instead of the traditional microphone when the AI is active.
  • If you've used Gemini before on your phone, on the web, or somewhere else, then you're going to know the extras that it brings over Google Assistant.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that google Assistant is being replaced by Google’s more advanced Gemini AI across all platforms, and that includes Android Auto. If the switch hasn’t happened yet on your own vehicle’s dashboard, then it should happen soon.

You’ll see a message onscreen announcing the arrival of Gemini, with the latest “spark” icon (a small star by a sound-wave-like icon), instead of the traditional microphone when the AI is active.

If you've used Gemini before on your phone, on the web, or somewhere else, then you're going to know the extras that it brings over Google Assistant. It's a truly natural conversation partner that can dig deep into information available online, and respond to a much wider range of queries. Here's what the upgraded app can do specifically when you're traveling on the road.

All of the standard commands you might have already been using are still here, of course, like "navigate home" or “Where's the nearest Walmart?” With Gemini though, there's much more flexibility in what you can say without the AI getting confused or misunderstanding what you're asking about.

For example, your questions can be multilayered. Something like "find the nearest coffee shop that has a drive-thru and is open now" will look for those exact criteria. You're also able to ask context-sensitive follow-up questions, such as "What time will it shut?" or "How long will it take to get there?" if you need further details.

It has been revealed that you can ask more general questions too, such as "tell me more about the place I'm heading to" or "Is there outdoor seating?” But bear in mind that Gemini will be limited to scouring the data on Google Maps for its information. (It's a disembodied AI that's never been anywhere.) If it doesn't know the answer to something, it should tell you that.

Overall, it's smarter in every aspect. I was recently navigating a difficult junction and couldn't work out whether the map was sending me left or right. I asked Gemini, "Will I be traveling east or west after the next turn?" and it figured out the answer. That helped me avoid veering off in the wrong direction.

One of the major benefits of having a voice-controlled AI in the car is having it handle messaging and audio tasks without you needing to take your eyes off the road or fish around for a button. If you tell Gemini to “read my last message,” it'll speak it out for you and give you the opportunity to reply. You can also specify the app, otherwise Google Messages will be used by default—Google Chat and WhatsApp are among the others that are supported.

It has been revealed that gemini is able to give you summaries of group chats, which is really handy when you're on a drive and the conversations you're involved in are building up message after message that you can't check. Name a group chat in a supported app and ask for a summary, or just request summaries of unread messages. You'll be able to get the gist without checking each individual message.

In a recent development, the usual array of audio commands are here, carried over from Google Assistant, so you can swiftly start or stop audio in your music, podcast, radio, and audiobook apps. As well as continuing from where you left off, you can also name artists, albums, and playlists that you want to queue up. YouTube Music and Spotify are among the apps supported, if you need to specify one.

Another extra from Gemini is being able to ask about the artist or song that's right now playing, and get more information on it. You might want to learn the history of a particular band, find out how long a certain song was at number one, or even get recommendations based on what's currently playing—just ask Gemini.

Much more than Google Assistant, Gemini can help you learn something or develop some ideas while you're behind the wheel. If you're on the way to a movie premiere, you can ask Gemini about the history of the film, the director, and the actors, and it'll remember the context of your conversation. (It'll all get synced back to the Gemini app on your other devices.).

Voice commands such as “help me prepare for my interview” or “come up with ideas for a quick and easy meal to make for dinner" will initiate a chat with Gemini that you can continue throughout your journey—and hopefully arrive well-prepared or with dinner sorted (or whatever it is). Maybe don’t ask about anything too mind-bending, as you’ll still need to concentrate on driving.

Gemini will ask along the way for any information it needs about what you’re interviewing for or the ingredients you’ve got at home. You can also ask Gemini to quiz you on a certain topic or run a query on something you see on the journey—like a landmark or a restaurant you go past.

Sources indicate that finally, there’s always the weather: Gemini will give you forecasts for the areas and specific locations you give it, on whatever day you want within the next week or so. Perhaps more useful for journeys are questions like “When is the rain going to stop?” or “What are the weather conditions like at my destination?” which will help you blueprint your trip.

U.S. officially loses measles elimination status amid ongoing outbreaks

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1027 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, the Pan American Health Organization unveiled the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence.
  • In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking fresh ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.

According to recent reports, the Pan American Health Organization unveiled the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission.

In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking fresh ones.

Industry observers note that "The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, noted during a news briefing on Tuesday.

Sources indicate that it's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.

More than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in Upcoming York and two in Wisconsin.

The commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas stated during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, noted Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action proposal in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation.

In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention noted it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status.

CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz remarked in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring.

Last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status.

According to recent reports, the decision also poses a latest test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence.

But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, said he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles.".

Sources indicate that "We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy mentioned. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.".

CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities.

Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.

The MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC demonstrates that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.

The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement.

Sources indicate that "We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood mentioned in a statement.

In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response.".

"We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," remarked Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America.

Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported.

Based on this year's case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

Recent findings suggest that the U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.

Chromosome ‘glue’ could boost fertility by stabilizing ageing eggs

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature
